---
title: "Your first brain-region predictions"
---

This tutorial takes you from an empty environment to a table of predicted brain regions,
and then to a plot of how the features vary along the probe.

It deliberately needs **no IBL account, no AWS credentials and no raw data of your own**.
Everything comes from a public Hugging Face repository, including a small bundled example
recording. By the end you will know how to load a published model, verify your install
reproduces it, run a prediction, and read the result.

Once you have that working, the [how-to guides](../how-to/compute-features-spikeglx.qmd)
show you how to swap in your own recording.

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.12 or newer
- Network access to the Hugging Face Hub. The decoder used here is about 30 MB — six
  XGBoost models plus the bundled example

## 1. Install

The lite install is all this tutorial needs — it includes model download and inference:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/int-brain-lab/ibleatools.git
cd ibleatools
pip install -e .
```

Check it imported:

```python
import ephysatlas

print(ephysatlas.__version__)
# 0.11.0 or later
```

## 2. Download a published model

There is one entry point for every model family: `load_pretrained`. Give it a Hugging Face
repository id, and pin a **revision** — a vintage tag such as `2026_W42`:

```python
from ephysatlas import load_pretrained

model = load_pretrained(
    "int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-xgboost", revision="2026_W42"
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Always pin a revision

Omit `revision=` and you get the `main` branch, which tracks the *currently recommended*
model and moves whenever a new vintage is published — so the same script can silently
return different regions next month. `load_pretrained` logs a warning when you do this.
Pin the tag and your result is reproducible.
:::

The download is verified against the checksums published alongside the model, so a
truncated or altered download fails loudly rather than quietly predicting nonsense.

## 3. Look at what you downloaded

Every published model ships a manifest, `ephysatlas_model.json`, and the wrapper exposes it
as `.index`. You never have to guess what a model consumes or emits:

```python
index = model.index

print(index["model_id"])            # 2026_W42_Cosmos_flimsy-thistle-cat
print(index["task"])                # region-classification
print(index["granularity"])         # channel
print(index["vintage"])             # 2026_W42

print(len(model.inputs["features"]))  # 48   — feature columns it needs
print(model.inputs["index"])          # ['pid', 'channel']
print(model.config["region_map"])     # Cosmos
print(model.config["class_acronyms"])
# ['void', 'MB', 'Isocortex', 'CB', 'TH', 'CNU', 'OLF', 'CTXsp', 'root', 'HB',
#  'HPF', 'HY', 'void_fluid']
```

So this model classifies each channel into one of 13 **Cosmos**-level regions, from 48
feature columns, on a table indexed by `(pid, channel)`.

## 4. Verify your install reproduces the model

Before trusting a single prediction, run the self-test. It re-predicts the example that
ships with the model and compares against the shipped expected output:

```python
model.selftest()
# True
```

This is the guard against version skew. A different XGBoost build, a NumPy upgrade that
changed a dtype, or features whose units moved between vintages all surface here as one
explicit failure — instead of showing up later as regions that are subtly, silently wrong.

Make this the first thing you run after any environment change.

## 5. Predict

The model bundles a small example feature table, so you can predict without any data of
your own:

```python
import pandas as pd

sample = model.path_model / "example" / "features_sample.parquet"
df = pd.read_parquet(sample)

print(df.shape[0])       # 500 — one row per channel
print(df.index.names)    # ['pid', 'channel']

out = model.predict(df)
```

## 6. Read the output

`predict` returns a DataFrame indexed exactly like its input:

```python
print(out[["predicted_acronym", "prediction_probability", "fold_agreement"]].head())
```

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `predicted_acronym` | Winning region, as an Allen acronym (`Isocortex`, `TH`, …) |
| `predicted_atlas_id` | The same region as a numeric Allen structure id |
| `prediction_probability` | Fold-averaged probability of the winning class |
| `fold_agreement` | Fraction of the 5 fold models that voted for the winner |
| `p_<acronym>` | One column per class, with its fold-averaged probability |

`fold_agreement` is the honest confidence signal. A channel with
`prediction_probability` of 0.6 but `fold_agreement` of 1.0 is a consistent call the model
is merely uncertain about; 0.6 with an agreement of 0.4 means the folds disagree, which is
a different and usually worse situation.

Summarise across the probe:

```python
print(out["predicted_acronym"].value_counts())

print(
    f"mean confidence {out['prediction_probability'].mean():.3f}, "
    f"mean fold agreement {out['fold_agreement'].mean():.3f}"
)
```

## 7. Join predictions back onto your features

The output columns are namespaced on purpose. Feature and cluster tables already carry
histology-derived `acronym` and `atlas_id` columns, so bare names would collide and
overwrite your ground truth. `predicted_*` never does:

```python
joined = df.join(out)
print(joined.shape)   # your feature columns, plus the prediction columns
```

If your table does carry histology labels, that join is exactly how you compare the
model's call against them.

## 8. Plot the features along the probe

Now look at the data the prediction came from. Features vary systematically with depth,
which is the whole reason a decoder works at all:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import ephysatlas.plots

fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.plot_features_distributions(
    df, x_list=["rms_lf", "psd_delta", "psd_gamma", "rms_ap", "spike_count"]
)
plt.show()
```

For the depth-resolved view — each feature as a colour-coded strip down the probe, beside
the brain regions — see
[plotting features along the probe](../how-to/plot-features-along-probe.qmd). That guide
needs channel coordinates (`x`, `y`, `z`, `axial_um`, `lateral_um`) alongside the features,
which the bundled sample does not carry.

## What's next?

You have run a published model end to end. To use it on your own recording you need to
produce a feature table in the shape this model expects — 48 named columns of
**denoised, aggregated** features. That is three steps:

1. [Compute features from your recording](../how-to/compute-features-spikeglx.qmd) — or
   from [NWB](../how-to/compute-features-nwb.qmd) /
   [Zarr](../how-to/compute-features-zarr.qmd) sources.
2. [Aggregate and denoise them](../how-to/aggregate-and-denoise.qmd) — a single snippet
   table is *not* what the model was trained on. For a SpikeGLX recording, steps 1 and 2
   are [one call](../how-to/compute-features-spikeglx.qmd#from-recording-to-brain-regions).
3. [Predict](../how-to/predict-regions.qmd), passing your own table instead of the sample.

Other directions:

- [Predict features from position](../how-to/predict-features-from-position.qmd) — the
  spatial encoder runs the other way round, turning coordinates into expected features.
- [Predict unit phenotypes from position](../how-to/predict-unit-phenotypes.qmd) — the
  same for spike-sorted units.
- [Core concepts](../explanation/concepts.qmd) — what a vintage is, and why denoising
  matters.
- [Model families](../explanation/model-families.qmd) — how the four families relate.
- [API reference](../api/index.qmd) — every parameter of everything above.
